title_r: Opening Pandora’s Box of GenAI in Management Research: IM Research Replication and Extension
abstract_r: This study asks if and how Generative AI (GenAI) simulations can be used as proxies and initial validation of empirical research, complementary to traditional methods of quantitative studies. This study explores the potential of Generative AI (GenAI) simulations as proxies for empirical research, complementing traditional quantitative methods. Using Entrepreneurial Orientation (EO) as the focal construct, we replicate Semrau, Ambos, and Sascha's (2016) study to evaluate the EO-performance relationship moderated by cultural contexts. Through AI-generated personas simulating SME senior managers across seven national contexts, we validate the replication’s consistency with the original study, confirming the universal applicability of EO in diverse cultural settings. The findings show that performance-based culture (PBC) significantly enhances the EO-performance relationship, while socially supportive culture (SSC) plays a marginal role, mirroring the original results. Furthermore, we extend the research by incorporating Individual Entrepreneurial Orientation (Ind.EO), demonstrating its strong predictive value for firm performance. The results highlight the potential of GenAI in cross-cultural research, offering a scalable, cost-effective, and culturally nuanced methodology. Our contributions are threefold: (1) validating GenAI as a tool for replication in social science research, (2) advancing methodological approaches by eliminating translation biases, and (3) extending EO frameworks with individual-level constructs. While limitations exist regarding GenAI’s depth of cultural understanding, the study underscores its transformative potential in refining and expanding empirical research practices.

title_r: The Dual Faces of Female Agency: A Replication and Extension Study
abstract_r: Female agency in professional settings is considered necessary, particularly in male-dominated contexts. However, based on expectancy violation perspective, existing studies also propose a backlash effect which indicating a negative response to agentic females. Other evidence, instead, shows that female agency can bring favorable ratings to females who exhibit agentic traits. The seminal work of Ma et al. (2022) reconciled these conflicting findings by differentiating prescriptive and proscriptive agency, suggesting that agency has a dual effect on females in terms of leadership. This study replicates and extends their findings in the entrepreneurial context. We confirm that prescriptive agency benefits females while proscriptive agency hinders females’ evaluations. We also find that this dual effect varies across managerial roles and entrepreneurial ones. Furthermore, we explore the underlying mechanism, showing that the different requirements for agency between management and entrepreneurship can explain that the positive side of agency is enhanced while negative side is attenuated among agentic female entrepreneurs compared to their manager peers. Through three pre-registered experiments, this study proves that their results are robust across two important settings for agentic females. These results have important implications for the theory and practice that we discuss.

title_r: Social media use for emotion regulation: A conceptual replication and extension.
abstract_r: Studies on emotion regulation (ER) have shown that people use various tools to shape their affective states. The present study used experience sampling method (ESM) to examine the impact of social media use on depressive symptoms and momentary negative affect among Japanese adults. Participants (Sample 1: 54 participants; Sample 2: 56 participants) reported social media use for ER and related psychological variables, five times each day for 7 consecutive days. We conducted identical surveys for Samples 1 and 2 to check for robustness of results; the present study was conducted in 2023. Results of multilevel analyses (lagged analyses) showed that most emotion regulatory social media uses were not significantly associated with depressive symptoms nor negative affect, suggesting that benefits of social media use may be scarce. However, cross-sectional analyses showed that few types of social media ER were associated with shifts toward desired emotional states. Considering that similar findings were reported in previous studies, these findings may suggest that effects of social media ER may be immediate or short-term across culture.

title_r: A Cross-sectional Conceptual Replication and Longitudinal Evaluation of the PANSS-Autism-Severity-Score Measure Suggests it Does Not Capture Autistic Traits in Individuals With Psychosis
abstract_r: BACKGROUND: Autism and psychosis co-occur at elevated rates, with implications for clinical outcomes, functioning, and suicidality. The PANSS-Autism-Severity-Score (PAUSS) is a measure of autism trait severity which has not yet been validated externally or longitudinally. STUDY DESIGN: Participants were derived from the GROUP and SCOPE datasets. Participants included 1448 adults with schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD), 800 SSD-siblings, 103 adults diagnosed with an autistic spectrum condition (ASC), and 409 typically-developing controls (TC). Analyses from the original validation study were conducted with SSD participants, and extended into ASC, SSD-sibling, and TC participants. Test-retest reliability of the PAUSS at 2-weeks and long-term stability 3 and 6-years was also examined. STUDY RESULTS: Results differed in important ways from the original validation. SSD participants reported higher PAUSS scores than other groups, with only a fraction of ASC participants scoring as "PAUSS-Autistic." Cronbach's alpha was acceptable for the SSD cohort only. Two-week stability of the PAUSS was fair to good for all PAUSS scores. Long-term stability was poor for most PAUSS items but fair for total PAUSS score. CONCLUSIONS: Results suggest that the PAUSS does not appear appropriate for assessing autism, with the low rate of PAUSS-Autistic in the ASC population suggesting the PAUSS may not accurately reflect characteristics of autism. The relative lack of long-term stability is cause for concern and suggestive that the PAUSS is capturing features of psychosis rather than autism traits.

title_r: People make inferences from policy decisions regarding default options: Replication and extension of McKenzie et al. (2006)
abstract_r: Default effect refers to the phenomenon that people tend to choose the default option in a choice-set. McKenzie et al. (2006) showed that one mechanism for the effect is that defaults are perceived as an implicit endorsement and a recommended option by the policy makers that set the defaults. In a pre-registered experiment with a Prolific online sample from the United States (N = 602), we conducted replications and extensions of Studies 1, 2, and 3 from McKenzie et al. (2006). We concluded a successful replication of all three studies, with support for their findings showing that: 1) people who are more willing to be organ donors are more likely to hold views that others should as well, and to think that enrollment should be the default, and that in turn: 2) people make inferences from policymaker’s set defaults (Study 2: organ donations; Study 3: retirement plans) regarding the policymakers’ own preferences regarding enrollment, and their views regarding whether others should enroll. In our extension we added a control condition with no defaults, finding that 1) people still make inferences about choice architects’ attitudes, even when defaults were not set, and 2) that setting defaults to not act (not enroll) is perceived as closer to no defaults than setting defaults to act (to enroll). Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/E5K4J.

abstract_r: In order to explore the mechanism behind the fact that people tend to hold overly favorable views of their abilities, Kruger and Dunning suggest that low metacognitive ability may result in cognitive bias by conducting a series of experiments. This study replicate and expand the key experiment of the original study and further put forward the potential influence that social comparison might has on the accuracy of self-evaluation from the collectivistic perspective. In the first study, incompetence subjects overestimated themselves and thus proved the cross-cultural robustness of Dunning-Kruger effect. In the second study, the subjects were asked to reassess themselves after observing the responses of the others. Neither high score group nor low score group showed significant difference between two assessments, which might be the result of the combined effects of metacognitive ability and social comparison.

title_r: Triplett’s Social Facilitation Experiment: A Registered Replication Report
abstract_r: A seminal study by Triplett provided initial evidence for the social facilitation effect, and over the last century research has demonstrated this effect across a range of settings. However, despite the importance of Triplett’s study no research has replicated the original study paradigm. Furthermore, in the context of research advances and methodological rigour, some elements of the original study weaken the validity of the observed findings. We address these critical limitations and replicate the original study, employing a standardized study protocol to minimise potential confounds, such as practice effects. A minimum of 400 school-aged children will be recruited. Using a purpose-built apparatus, participants will complete each trial twice — once alone and once in competition with another participant. Trial order will be standardized. The results of this study will extend research on social facilitation by replicating the original study paradigm and exploring potential age and gender effects.

title_r: SPR 2019 Symposium: Methodological Rigor and Multi-Site Replications in Psychophysiology
abstract_r: The reproducibility, replicability, and robustness of findings in psychological science have led to a perceived crisis. The purpose of this symposium is to identify barriers to the replicability of psychophysiological data and to provide recommendations for improving psychophysiology research practices. The symposium begins with Carbine reporting the sample sizes and statistical power that are common in studies of event-related brain potentials (ERPs) and highlighting the importance of a priori power calculations. Clayson then discusses how researchers are not reporting all the necessary data collection and processing steps outlined in the ERP methodology guidelines published in 2014, which is a barrier to replication studies. Sandre provides an example of the impact of various processing pipelines on error-related negativity (ERN) scores, psychometrics, and relationships with external correlates. One recommendation for improving replicability and robustness of research to is to conduct large multi-site studies. The symposium concludes with two presentations that cover the results and challenges of such studies. Bauer presents on a multi-site replication of the relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and threat generalization using skin conductance responses (SCR) and ERPs. Moser reports on a multi-site replication of the relationship between ERN and worry. Together, these presentations highlight challenges to the reproducibility, replicability, and robustness of psychophysiological findings and provide recommendations for best practices moving forward.

title_r: norm replication / status quo and policy support
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The first part of this study replicates a prior study examining the relationship between social norms and people's perception of what behaviors come to mind as desirable and possible to do in a given situation. Key outcome is a correlation between perceptions of the norm surrounding a given behavior in a given situation, and the degree to which people say that behavior would be likely to 'come to mind' if they were experiencing some relevant motivational state. Second key outcome is the same correlation for ratings of how much participants would 'want to' do the behavior.

The other part of this study examines whether behavior change policies that are already in place receive greater support than policies that have merely been proposed. In addition to hypothesizing that 'enacted' policies will receive more popular support than 'proposed' policies, I hypothesize that 'proposed' policies will be viewed as less beneficial to individuals and society, and as more of an infringement on freedom, than 'enacted' policies. 
In a secondary part of this study, I ask people to evaluate another set of policies that are already in place in the US, again hypothesizing that support for already-existing policies will be higher than for proposed policies. 

Primary outcome is change in these variables on a 7 point scale. I will also compute dichotomized variables (e.g. percentage of respondents supporting a policy, or agreeing that it is an infringement on freedom) for descriptive purposes. 

Secondary analyses will examine whether and how these effects interact with participant party ID. 

Sample size is 1000, set in advance by funder. 
Data will be collected by Lucid. 
Exclusion criteria are: 
- Subject spends less than 240 seconds completing the task
- Subject indicates that they were distracted or answering randomly on an attention check question.

Full materials and initial analysis plan are uploaded.

title_r: Colorblind ideology/Assimilation and Perception of a Bleak Future on Anti-immigration attitudes and White Nationalism: Replication and Extensions
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

In our first pre-registered study titled “Re-categorization and Perception of a Bleak Future”, we assess whether (1) the perception of a bleak future for one’s racial group by the majority (Whites) will predict anti-immigration policies, (2) not recategorizing targets of prejudice as having a shared identity will lead Whites to show higher anti-immigration attitudes, especially when they perceive a bleak future. Our analysis showed that anti-immigration attitudes were not dependent on recategorizations, i.e participants who recategorized and those who did not showed higher anti-immigration attitudes when they perceived a bleak future. However, the trend for low recategorizers was more steep than for the high recatgeorizers. Hence, the effect of perceived bleak future on anti-immigration attitudes was more pronounced in low recategorizers. In our previous study, we acknowledge that the item we used to measure recategorization was actually a measure of assimilation (a facet of colorblindness) which explains the result. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to see if the result found in our earlier study would replicate using explicit measures of color blind ideology (CBI)/assimilation. We expect a similar pattern with support for white nationalist ideologies.

title_r: Effectiveness of a numeracy intelligent tutoring system in kindergarten: A conceptual replication
abstract_r: Intelligent Tutoring Systems are a genre of highly adaptive software providing individualized instruction. The current study was a conceptual replication of a previous randomized control trial that incorporated the intelligent tutoring system Native Numbers, a program designed for early numeracy instruction. As a conceptual replication, we kept the method of instruction, the demographics, the number of kindergarten classrooms (n = 3), and the same numeracy and intrinsic motivation screeners as the original study. We changed the time of year of instruction, changed the control group to a wait-control group, added a maintenance assessment for the first group of participants, and included a mathematical language assessment. Analysis of within- and between-group differences using repeated measures ANOVA indicated gains of numeracy were significant only after using Native Numbers (Partial Eta Square = 0.147). Results of intrinsic motivation and mathematical language were not significant. The effect size of numeracy achievement did not reach that of the original study (Partial Eta Square = 0.622). Here, we compared the two studies, discussed plausible reasons for differences in the magnitude of effect sizes, and provided suggestions for future research.

title_r: Open-label placebo effects on psychological and physical well-being: a conceptual replication study
abstract_r: Background: Contrary to traditional placebos, open-label placebos (OLP) abstain from deception, i.e., participants are openly informed to receive an inert substance. Studies in clinical and healthy samples evidence the efficacy of OLPs. This study aims to conceptually replicate and expand findings of a recent OLP study in healthy participants while implementing a within-subject design and daily instead of retrospective assessments. Additionally, the effect of a brand name on the medicine container is tested and possible predictors of the OLP effects are explored. Methods: Healthy participants (N = 75) received OLP and no placebo for 5 days each (randomized sequence) and answered daily questionnaires on sleep quality, bodily symptoms, mental well-being, and psychological distress. The medicine container of half the participants had a brand name, the remaining did not. Different personality traits and situational factors were assessed. Results: Mental and physical well-being did not differ between OLP and control phase, i.e., overall, no OLP effect emerged. Contrast analysis indicated that an OLP effect emerged for sleep quality and psychological distress when no brand name was present. Further, an OLP effect emerged in persons with higher expectations for bodily symptoms (r = .23, p = .046) and psychological distress (r = .24, p = .037). Conclusions: Methodological differences to the original study are discussed as an explanation for the failure to induce overall OLP effects. Future studies should continue to replicate previous findings and determine the exact conditions of successful implementation of OLP effects in healthy as well as clinical samples.

title_r: TESS Experiments: Proposal to Replicate and Extend Seven TESS Studies - Part 2
abstract_r: Time-sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS) offers researchers the opportunity to capture the internal validity of experiments. Investigators submit proposals, and TESS fields successful proposals for free on a representative sample of adults in the United States. This 2-wave multi-experiment study was conducted to test the persistence of framing effects. In experiment 1, Wave 1 respondents were randomly assigned to one of three framing treatments in which they were asked to read an article on the popularity of a television show (Control), partisan agreement, or political polarization. Respondents then indicated their stance and what they believed the stance of the typical Democratic and Republican voter would be, on capital gains taxes, undocumented immigrants, free-trade agreements, and election financing. In experiment 2, Wave 1 respondents were randomly assigned to one of eight conditions which varied arguments presented for or against international trade (none (Control), pro, con, or both pro and con) and either omitted or included expert consensus on the benefit of and need to increase international trade. Respondents were then asked to report their support/non-support of increased international trade. A total of 2,123 respondents participated in Wave 1. Wave 2 (n=1865) resurveyed respondents 10 days later. This allowed for comparison of immediate and longer-term effects of framing.

title_r: Corporate entrepreneurship and firm performance relationship under the moderating effect of environmental dynamism: Replication and extension analysis
abstract_r: Abstract The purpose of this research is to understand the relationship between corporate entrepreneurship and firm performance of large firms in emerging economies, with consideration of the moderating effect of environmental dynamism. This is a quantitative and cross-sectional study, utilizing a multivariate second-order hierarchical component model. The partial least squares structural equation modeling method was employed for analysis. The findings indicate a highly positive impact of entrepreneurial orientation on profitability, while corporate venturing had a high but negative impact on profitability. Regarding the growth model, it was shown that entrepreneurial orientation had a positive but statistically insignificant impact on firm growth, while corporate venturing had a highly negative but statistically insignificant impact on firm growth. Interestingly, the results indicate that environmental dynamism did not have a moderating effect in this context. This paper has significant implications for senior management decision-making regarding the importance of corporate entrepreneurship in the growth and profitability of companies. It is recommended that large companies invest in entrepreneurial orientation because of its positive influence on profitability. This research fills a gap in the literature on the relationship between corporate entrepreneurship and firm performance in large companies in emerging economies. It highlights the importance of context-specific contingencies to the impact of corporate entrepreneurship on the performance of large companies and cautions against generalizing results across different countries, even those with seemingly similar contexts. The study confirms the positive relationship between entrepreneurial orientation and corporate profitability, particularly for large companies.

title_r: People react more positively to female- than to male-favoring sex differences: A direct replication of a counterintuitive finding
abstract_r: We report a direct replication of our earlier study looking at how people react to research on sex differences depending on whether the research puts men or women in a better light. Three-hundred-and-three participants read a fictional popular-science article about fabricated research finding that women score higher on a desirable trait/lower on an undesirable one (female-favoring difference) or that men do (male-favoring difference). Consistent with our original study, both sexes reacted less positively to the male-favoring differences, with no difference between men and women in the strength of this effect. Also consistent with our original study, belief in male privilege and a left-leaning political orientation predicted less positive reactions to the male-favoring sex differences; neither variable, however, predicted reactions to the female-favoring sex differences (in the original study, male-privilege belief predicted positive reactions). As well as looking at how participants reacted to the research, we looked at their predictions about how the average man and woman would react. Consistent with our earlier results, participants of both sexes predicted that the average man and woman would exhibit considerable own-sex favoritism. In doing so, they exaggerated the magnitude of the average woman's own-sex favoritism and predicted strong own-sex favoritism from the average man when in fact the average man exhibited modest other-sex favoritism. A greater awareness of people's tendency to exaggerate own-sex bias could help to ameliorate conflict between the sexes.

abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Numerous studies have shown that the activation of negative stereotypes can have detrimental effects on group members’ performance (i.e., stereotype threat effect). However, much less is known about the impact of stereotype threat beyond performance. In the present research, we examined the effects of stereotype threat on the motivational aspects of subsequent interpersonal interactions (i.e., social approach motivation). Specifically, based on earlier work showing that being negatively stereotyped can lead to uncertainty about one’s belonging to relevant groups, we hypothesized that activating negative stereotypes reduces motivation to approach these groups via reduced sense of belonging.  In the current study, we aim to replicate our previous experimental study (N = 140) that demonstrated that the activation of a negative stereotype (i.e., women have less ability in math than men) leads to reduced social approach motivation in female university students via reduced sense of belonging.  In addition, we include a group of male university students to prove that the effect is different for females and males.  Specifically, we hypothesize that the effect of the negative stereotype that women have less ability in math than men will affect female (but not male) students’ social approach motivation and that this effect is mediated by reduced sense of belonging to the university and other students.  Finally, although we assess both social approach and avoidance motivation as outcome variables, we assume that – as in our previous study – social approach (compared to avoidance) motivation is more sensitive to signals indicating a lack of social integration in young adults (as might be the case after the activation of negative stereotypes).

title_r: An experimental replication and extension to “sexual communal motivation and self-determined sexual motivation in romantic relationships”
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The following pre-registered study is an experimental replication and extension of previous studies in this project

summary: 1) Hypotheses. What are the main question being asked or hypotheses being tested in this study?

Communal theories of sexual motivation suggest that romantic partners experience higher satisfaction and desire when they are responsive to each other’s sexual needs (i.e., high sexual communal strength); however, doing so at the expense of attending to one’s own sexual needs (i.e., high unmitigated sexual communion) has been associated with mixed outcomes. To distinguish sexual communal strength from unmitigated sexual communion, we are interested in examining whether autonomous sexual motives (i.e., inherently choiceful and meaningful) and controlled motives (i.e., pressured and obligated) for engaging in sex mediate the effects of sexual communal strength and unmitigated sexual communion on relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction, and desire. 

In two cross sectional studies—one with people in relationships and the other with couples—we found that people higher in sexual communal strength and their partners endorsed more autonomous sexual motivation, and in turn reported higher relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction, and sexual desire. In contrast, people higher in unmitigated sexual communion and their partners endorsed more controlled sexual motivation and in turn reported lower satisfaction and desire. 

The current pre-registration is for an experimental study designed to manipulate sexual communal motivation (i.e., sexual communal strength vs. unmitigated sexual communal vs. control) using a false feedback paradigm and to test whether autonomous and controlled sexual motives mediate the associations between sexual communal motivation and sexual and relationship outcomes. To manipulate sexual communal motivation, we will provide participants with false feedback about their levels of responsiveness to their partner’s sexual needs as well as their levels of assertiveness with their own sexual needs. Participants will either be oriented to high sexual communal strength (i.e., provided with feedback about their high responsiveness to a partner’s needs + high assertiveness of own needs), high unmitigated sexual communion (i.e., provided with feedback about their high responsiveness + low assertiveness), or receive no feedback (i.e., control). Relative to participants in the unmitigated sexual communion and control conditions, we expect that people in the sexual communal strength condition will endorse more autonomous sexual motives and less controlled sexual motives, and in turn, will report greater satisfaction and desire. Compared to participants in the control condition, those in the unmitigated sexual communion condition will endorse less autonomous sexual motives and more controlled sexual motives, and in turn report poorer sexual and relational outcomes.

2) Independent variable. Describe the key independent variable(s) specifying how they were measured.

The primary independent variable, sexual communal motivation, will be manipulated. However, we will include the following baseline measures as potential covariates and moderators for secondary analyses.

Baseline measures 

Sexual communal motivation. Sexual communal strength (Muise, Impett, Kogan, & Desmarais, 2013) will be assessed with 6 items (e.g., How far would you be willing to go to meet your partner's sexual needs?) using a 5-point Likert scale (0 = not at all to 4 = extremely). Unmitigated sexual communion will be measured with 7 items (e.g., I always place my partner’s sexual needs above my own) using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree).

Sexual assertiveness. Sexual assertiveness will be measured with the sexual assertiveness subscale of the Multidimensional Sexual Self-Concept Questionnaire (Snell, 1998). Participants rate their sexual assertiveness with 5 items (e.g., “I am very assertive about the sexual aspects of my life.”) using a 5-point Likert scale (1= not at all characteristic of me to 5= very characteristic of me)

Relationship satisfaction.  Relationship satisfaction will be measured with the 16-item version of the Couple Satisfaction Index (Funk & Rogge, 2007). Participants rate their relationship satisfaction with their partner (e.g., “In general, how often do you think that things between you and your partner are going well?”), on 5-point scales with anchors tailored to specific items (e.g., 0 = never, 5 = All the time)

Sexual satisfaction. Sexual satisfaction will be measured with the Global Measure of Sexual Satisfaction (Lawrence & Byers, 1998). Participants’ rate their sexual satisfaction with five bipolar items on a 7-point scale (e.g., My sex life is “very bad” to “very good”).

Sexual desire: Sexual desire will be measured with the dyadic subscale of the Sexual Desire Inventory-2 (Spector, Carey & Steinberg, 1996). Participants rate their sexual desire for their partner with seven items (e.g., “When you have sexual thoughts, how strong is your desire to engage in sexual behaviour with a partner?”) on 9-point scales with anchors tailored to specific items (e.g., 0 = no desire, 8 = strong desire).

3) Dependent variable. Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they were measured.

Self-determined sexual motivation. Nine items were adapted from the Sexual Motivation Scale (SMS; Gravel, Pelletier, & Reissing, 2016) to measure participants’ current autonomous motivation (4 items., e.g., “Because I feel that having sex is meaningful.”) and controlled motivation (5 items, e.g., “To prove to myself that I am a good lover.”) to engage in sex, on a 7-point scale (1=Not at all, 7= Extremely).

Relationship satisfaction. Relationship satisfaction will be measured with the 4 item Couple Satisfaction Index(see above) and adapted aft to reflect participants’ relationship satisfaction at the present moment (i.e., “right now”).

Sexual Satisfaction. Sexual satisfaction will be measured with the Global Measure of Sexual Satisfaction (see above) and adapted to reflect participants’ sexual satisfaction at the present moment (i.e., “right now”). 

Sexual desire. Sexual desire will be measured with one item (“I feel a great deal of sexual desire for my partner right now.” using a 7-point scale (1=Not at all, 7= Extremely).

4) Conditions. How many and which conditions were participants assigned to?

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three conditions. Based on a false feedback paradigm previously used in relationship and sexuality research (Balzarini et al., 2021; Maxwell et al., 2017) participants will receive false feedback about their levels of sexual responsiveness and sexual assertiveness in their relationship under the guise of an algorithm that calculated results from participant’s baseline measures, which in reality are ostensible scores used to manipulate sexual communal motivation. Participants will be randomly assigned to the sexual communal strength (i.e., high sexual responsiveness + high sexual assertiveness), unmitigated sexual communion (i.e., high sexual responsiveness + low sexual assertiveness) or the control (i.e., no false feedback) conditions. 

A pilot study was conducted to test the sexual communal motivation manipulation. The sample for the pilot study included 150 participants recruited from Prolific, an online crowd sourcing platform, who were in a relationship for at least 6 months, sexually active, and 18 years or older. After the manipulation, participants responded to one item manipulation checks measuring their sexual responsiveness (“To what extent are you responsive to your partner’s sexual needs?”) and sexual assertiveness (“To what extent are you assertive with your own sexual needs?), using a 7-point scale (1=Not at all, 7= Extremely). There was a significant effect of condition on both sexual responsiveness (F2,147 = 3.217, p = .043, ηp2  = .042) and sexual assertiveness (F2,147 = 25.55, p <. 001, ηp2  = .26). Post hoc analyses with a Tukey adjustment revealed that participants in the SCS condition (M = 5.96, SD = .96) reported significantly higher sexual responsiveness (t = .50, SE = .21, p =.045) than the control condition (M = 5.46, SD = 1.20). There were no significant differences between SCS and USC (t = .10, SE = .21, p = .87), which was expected given that they were both manipulating high responsiveness. However, there was also no significant difference between USC and control (t = .40, SE = .21, p =.15) on sexual responsiveness, but the mean responsiveness score was higher in the USC condition (M =5.86, SD= .96) compared to control. Participants in the SCS condition (M = 5.14, SD = 1.31) reported being significantly more sexually assertive than those in the USC (t = 1.85, SE = .26, p < .001) and control (t =.62, SE = .26, p= .051) conditions as expected. Participants in the USC condition (M = 3.29, SD = 1.32) also reported less sexual assertiveness (t = -1.23, SE =.27, p <.001) than those in the control condition (M = 4.52, SD = 1.31). Overall, the pilot study suggested that our manipulation was successful in shifting people’s feelings of sexual responsiveness and assertiveness as intended. 

Participants in the SCS and USC conditions also responded to item gauging the accuracy and believability of feedback in terms of sexual responsiveness (e.g., “The feedback accurately captured my levels of sexual responsiveness” and sexual assertiveness (e.g., “The feedback accurately captured my levels of sexual assertiveness”). The effects of condition on sexual responsiveness and sexual assertiveness were not significant (F1,98 = .0.43, p = .836; F1,98 = .2.24, p = .137). Although participants in the SCS and USC conditions did not statistically differ on the extent to which they believed the feedback, the average scores in both conditions were relatively high for both sexual responsiveness (M = 5.55, SD = 1.46; M = 5.49, SD = 1.39) and sexual assertiveness (M = 5.25, SD = 1.53; M = 4.76, SD = 1.80). Additionally, only a small number of people guessed the hypothesis (4.6%) based on open ended responses (e.g., “What do you think this study is about?”; “Do you have any comments about the study in general?”), suggesting that overall, the manipulation was believable. 

5) Analyses. Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct to examine the main question/hypothesis.

We will use Hayes’s (2013) SPSS macro-PROCESS (Model 6) with 95% bias corrected confidence interval (CIs) based on 20,000 bootstrap samples to test for total, direct, and indirect effects in our proposed mediation models. Sexual communal motivation will be entered as a multicategorical independent variable in the model (Hayes & Preacher, 2014) with the control condition as the reference group for comparisons with the sexual communal strength and unmitigated sexual communion conditions. The unmitigated sexual communion condition as the reference group for the comparison with the sexual communal strength condition. Autonomous and controlled sexual motives will be simultaneously entered as mediators in the model.

6) More analyses. Any secondary analyses?

We will test for differences across groups in key demographics such as age and relationship length. If these differ across groups, we will control for them in subsequent analyses. We can also assess if any of the primary effects are moderated by participants’ baseline sexual communal strength, unmitigated sexual communion, sexual assertiveness, relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction, and sexual desire reported at baseline.

7) Sample Size. How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size?

In the pilot study, we also included one of our key outcomes—sexual satisfaction—in order to provide an estimate of the effect size. A small to medium effect of condition on sexual satisfaction was found (ηp2  = .048). We then used this estimate as the effect of condition on the account and the correlations from our previous study (ranging from +/- .58 to .17) for the associations with the mediators variables to input into a monte carlo power analysis for our proposed model with parallel mediators (Schoemann, Boulton, & Short, 2017). The power analysis indicated that 500 participants would be needed to estimate a small to medium effect with 80% power. To account for incomplete surveys and exclusion criteria, we will oversample by 20% to account for the potential exclusion of inattentive responders, participants who do not believe the false feedback based on open-ended responses, and those who are outliers on our key outcomes. Approximately 600 participants will be recruited from Prolific. To be eligible for this study, individuals will have to provide informed consent, be 18 years or older, be involved in a romantic relationship of at least six months and be sexually active with their partner.

8) Other. Anything else you would like to pre-register?

Based on an open-ended question provided after the manipulated feedback (“Please tell us what the results say about your levels of sexual responsiveness and assertiveness with your partner?”, we will exclude participants who did not know what the feedback was or indicated that they did not believe the feedback. Participants who indicate that they were provided false feedback or similar responses on two open ended questions at the end of the study (e.g., “What do you think this study is about?”; “Do you have any comments about the study in general?”) will be excluded. We will launch the study with a small batch of ten participants first and review their open-ended responses to ensure no issues with the survey. If no issues arise, we will launch the full study including the earlier batch. If the responses alert us to any changes, we will make these and do another launch (and not include the first batch).

Participants who reported paying “no attention” or “little attention” on an attention check question at the end of the study will also be excluded. Participants who reported that they did not complete the study honestly on a question at the end of the study will also be excluded. Lastly, participants will be excluded from analyses if they respond +/- 2.5 standard deviations on the primary dependent variables.

9) Name. Give a title for this pre-registration
An experimental replication and extension to “sexual communal motivation and self-determined sexual motivation in romantic relationships”

title_r: Preregistration of replication and extension study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

In humans, attitudes can be learned when initially neutral stimuli (Conditioned Stimuli, CSs), such as faces of unfamiliar persons or brand names, are merely presented together (i.e., paired) with valent stimuli (Unconditioning Stimuli, USs), for example beautiful faces or pleasant scene images (Hofmann, De Houwer, Perugini, Baeyens, & Crombez, 2010). It is debated whether this phenomenon—evaluative conditioning (EC)—can occur unconsciously. While there is little evidence supporting EC in the absence of awareness during learning (for review, see Corneille & Stahl, 2019), some studies report EC in the absence of participants’ memory of the CS-US pairing at the time of retrieval (e.g., Hütter, Sweldens, Stahl, Unkelbach, & Klauer, 2012; Waroquier, Abadie, & Dienes, 2020).

In a recent study, Stahl, Aust, Mierop, Béna, and Corneille (2020) used an improved assessment procedure and came to the opposite conclusion: In their study, whenever participants reported not remembering the valence of the US, they did not show EC effects. This finding suggests that EC and memory are strongly related, and that there is no EC in the absence of memory. Here we aim at replicating this finding with a larger sample.

A second goal of this study is to extend the study of the EC-memory relation by asking, reversely, whether there is memory in the absence of attitudes towards the CS. If EC and
memory are tightly related, then participants should always have acquired an attitude whenever they remember a CS-US pairing. If, on the other hand, CS-US pairing memory is
merely a precondition for establishing an attitude, one would expect to find cases of memory without learned attitudes.

title_r: Social Distance and Preference for Visual and Verbal Mediums in Interpersonal Communication: A Conceptual Replication of Amit et al. (2013, Experiment 2)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The present study aims to conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope’s (2013, Experiment 2) study, which explored the effect of social (psychological) distance on peoples’ medium preferences for interpersonal communication. The results showed that participants preferred mediums dominated by pictures for socially ‘close’ targets and mediums dominated by words for socially ‘distant’ targets. These findings support construal level theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010) which propose that people use more abstract representations when mentalizing targets that are more psychologically distant. The current study will conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope (2013, Experiment 2) to assess the robustness of the original conclusions by using a set of new pretested experimental materials.

abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Replication of Rochefort et al. (2017) on Discriminant Validity of AAQ-II and MEAQ from Neuroticism/Negative Affect 
Study Registration

Research Questions: 
1. Do the most commonly used measures of experiential avoidance (MEAQ and AAQ-II) demonstrate appropriate discriminant validity from neuroticism (IPIP-NEO-N and BFI-2-N) and trait negative affect (TAI) at the scale, subscale, and item levels? 

2. Are the results from Rochefort et al. (2017) replicable using different neuroticism and trait negative affect measures? 

Hypothesis:
We hypothesize that the AAQ-II will continue to be overly saturated with neuroticism and trait negative affect variance, such that it will function as an indicator of neuroticism and negative affect instead of experiential avoidance at the scale, subscale, and item levels. In addition, we hypothesize that the MEAQ will demonstrate appropriate discriminate validity from neuroticism and negative affect, and will demonstrate appropriate associations with another third-wave behavior therapy construct, mindfulness. 

Participants and Recruitment Method: 
We are planning to collect cross-sectional data from 500 adult participants recruited from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk and a minimum of 300 undergraduates. In recruiting undergraduate participants, we will not stop data collection at 300 participants, but will instead continue to collect data until the end of the semester in which we reach 300 participants. 

Procedure and Measures: 
Participants will complete questionnaires online, including the Multidimensional Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (MEAQ), the Action and Acceptance Questionnaire-2 (AAQ-II), IPIP-NEO Neuroticism scale (IPIP-NEO-N), Big Five Inventory-2 Neuroticism scale (BFI-2-N), Temperament and Affectivity Inventory (TAI), and the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ). 

Analytic Overview:
Similar to the analyses conducted in Rochefort et al. (2017), we will:
	- Examine Pearson correlations between all scales and subscales
	- Conduct significance tests for dependent correlations to determine differences in strength between the correlations
	- Conduct exploratory factor analyses with promax rotation at the scale, subscale, and item levels 
	- Conduct parallel analyses to determine the maximum number of factors to extract in the scale, subscale, and item level extractions
	- Present item level results using Goldberg’s (2006) bassackward approach 
	- Conduct exploratory structural equation modeling to determine the optimal solutions at the scale, subscale, and item levels 
All analyses will be conducted in the MTurk and undergraduate student samples separately in order to examine replication of our results.

title_r: Replication and Extension of KIN TECH 2.0: Randomized Controlled Trial of Kinship Navigation in Florida
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This study will test if a community-based kinship navigator program will reduce the incidence of a substantiated child maltreatment event at 12 and 36 months follow up. Core components of KIN TECH 2.0 include: 1) intake and assessment of family needs; 2) connection to community resources and supports; 3) assistance with application and enrollment to resources; 4) peer-to-peer support; 5) problem-solving with interdisciplinary team (IDT); and 6) follow-up. The intervention includes an intake phone session, weekly phone/in-person intervention for up to 12 weeks, and two follow-up post-intervention check ins at 12 and 36 months. The Control Group will receive Usual Child Welfare Service services and supports currently available to the community-based care organization in Hillsborough County when children are placed in the home of relatives. The participants in the Usual Care group will receive the following: 1) a packet of information explaining available services and supports, 2) a home study to ensure the environment is safe for the child, 3) in-home case management for the relative child, and 4) an opportunity to become a licensed foster home or Permanent Guardianship Placement. Both the intervention and control group interventions are administered by different organizations working on a contract to deliver
services. During the planning phase, the study team will spend time interviewing child welfare staff and collecting data on how usual care is implemented at this particular time. We also plan to monitor this usual care group over time to ensure that there is no creep into the intervention. 

This seven-year study will have four phases, including: (1) a 9-month study planning phase, (2) a 27 month enrollment and random assignment phase, (3) a 51 month follow-up and data collection phase, starting 12 months after the start of enrolment and finishing 36 months after the end of the enrolment/random assignment phase, and (4) a 12 month data analysis and dissemination phase. We anticipate enrolling 600 kinship caregivers who will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: 1) a KIN-TECH group or 2) a usual care (child welfare as usual). The primary outcome measure will be safety operationalized by subsequent maltreatment from random assignment and follow up in 12- and 36-months. Subsequent maltreatment events are hypothesized to decrease with KIN-TECH compared to the usual care group. We will be using the child identification number, as we used in previous study, in the State Administered database, Florida Safe Families Network (FSFN), to track the proportion of children in the study who have experienced a substantiated maltreatment event by the 12 and 36 month follow up. To detect small differences between the two groups, using a t-test from an ANCOVA estimating cross-sectional impacts at each point of view at followof 0.80, the sample size needed in each group is approximately 300 for a total crude sample size of 600.

title_r: Resting state cortico-limbic functional connectivity and dispositional use of emotion regulation strategies: A replication and extension study
abstract_r: Neuroimaging functional connectivity analyses have shown that the negative coupling between amygdala and cortical regions is linked to better emotion regulation (ER) in experimental task settings. However, less is known about the neural correlates of ER traits or dispositions. The present study aimed to (1) replicate the findings of differential cortico-limbic coupling during resting state depending on the dispositional use of ER strategies. Furthermore, the study aimed to (2) extend prior findings by examining whether differences in cortico-limbic coupling during resting state predict behavioral and neuronal emotion regulation success in a standard emotion regulation task. To this end, N=107 healthy adults completed the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ), underwent an 8-min resting-state fMRI acquisition and completed a reappraisal task during fMRI. Functional connectivity maps of basolateral and centromedial amygdala nuclei were estimated with a seed-based approach regarding associations with regions of the prefrontal cortex, and were then correlated with ERQ scores as well as behavioral and neuronal ER success. All hypotheses and the analysis plan are preregistered at https://osf.io/8wsgu. Opposed to prior findings, we were not able to replicate a correlation of habitual ER strategy use with functional connectivity between amygdala and PFC regions. Furthermore, there was no association of behavioral and neuronal reappraisal success with functional connectivity between amygdala and insula as well as PFC. The present preregistered study calls into question the reported association between individual differences in resting state cortico-limbic connectivity and habitual use of ER strategies. However, ongoing advances in functional brain imaging and distributed network approaches may leverage the identification of reliable functional connectivity patterns that underlie successful emotion regulation.

title_r: The effect of prompts on the sharing of news headlines in social media: a pre-registered replication study of Capraro and Celadin (2023).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Misinformation, such as fake news and conspiracy theories, is contaminated among information on the internet. Specifically, research has found that 40% of information in the medical domain from the internet has been found to be misinformation (Waszak et al., 2018).
Today, various studies are being conducted to help prevent the spread of such misinformation. For example, increasing the sharing of accurate information by having people assess the accuracy of another article before a sharing task (Pennycook et al., 2020) or giving simple online literacy tips can reduce the sharing of misinformation (Epstein et al., 2021). Such methods of manipulating sharing on SNSs have been demonstrated.
However, while misinformation can be reduced, it is challenging to encourage the sharing of correct information. Capraro and Celadin (2023) found that adding a short sentence (prompt) to the 'share' option presented in the sharing task increased the sharing of correct information and reduced the sharing of misinformation. However, the participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, resulting in a biased sample. Therefore, to confirm the generalizability of Capraro and Celadin’s (2023) findings, the present study will conduct a replication study using a different sample to examine the viability of a method that promotes sharing of correct information and reduces the sharing of misinformation.

summary: Study Information
Title (required)
Provide the working title of your study. It is helpful if this is the same title that you submit for publication of your final manuscript, but it is not a requirement.
10-month-old infants’ social evaluation of true versus negligent accidents: A direct replication attempt
Authors (required)
The author who submits the preregistration is the recipient of the award money and must also be an author of the published manuscript. Additional authors may be added or removed at any time.
Brandon M. Woo & J. Kiley Hamlin
Research Questions (required)
Please list each research question included in this study.
Our goal is to reassess 10-month-old infants’ evaluation of truly accidental versus negligently accidental helpers and harmers. In a past study (see Woo, Steckler, Le, & Hamlin, under revised review), we found that infants preferred a truly accidental over a negligently accidental harmer, but did not distinguish between truly and negligently accidental helpers. This asymmetry between how infants evaluate negligently accidental help and harm, if reliable, would be consistent with the side-effect effect, whereby adults and children age 4 and 5 attribute intentionality to foreseen harm but not to foreseen help (Knobe, 2003; Leslie et al., 2006; for similar evidence with infants, see Hamlin & Baron, 2014). However, the nature of this asymmetry is currently somewhat unclear: In the original study, whereas infants’ preference for negligently accidental versus truly accidental helpers did not reach significance, more infants chose a negligently accidental helper than chose a truly accidental helper (that is, the pattern of results was in the hypothesized direction, but did not reach significance). Thus, it may be that infants attribute helpful intention to negligently accidental helpers, but to a lesser extent than they attribute harmful intention to negligently accidental harmers. Alternatively, it may be that infants do not attribute helpful intention to negligently accidental helpers at all. Finally, it may also be possible that the asymmetry we initially observed was a statistical fluke. The present study is an attempt to replicate this promising result. We will use a sample size based on a power analysis with the observed effect sizes in the work of Woo et al. (under revised review).
We will test infants in a puppet show paradigm centered around a tiger protagonist’s goal involving a shelf; this is the exact same paradigm from the original study (see Woo et al., under revised review). Infants will be randomly sorted into one of two conditions: help and harm. In both conditions, there will be a shelf with a duck toy in front of it.
In the helping condition, the tiger will have an unfulfilled goal to reach a moose toy on the top of the shelf. After infants see the tiger try to reach the moose, infants will see two dog actors in alternating trials, running to the duck toy and knocking the shelf over as a side-effect of their own goal to reach the duck toy. The shelf’s falling over will enable the tiger to reach the moose. Critically, one of the dogs will have been on stage to witness and gain knowledge of the tiger’s attempts to reach the moose toy, and will therefore be negligently accidental in its behavior (i.e., it could have foreseen the positive consequences that its actions would have for the tiger). The other dog will not be on stage during the tiger’s attempts to reach the moose, and will therefore be truly accidental in its behavior (i.e., it could not have foreseen the consequences).
In the harming condition, the tiger will have a goal to place a moose toy on the top of the shelf. After infants see the tiger successfully place the moose on the top of the shelf, infants will see two dog actors in alternating trials, running to the duck toy and knocking the shelf over as a side-effect of their own goal to reach the duck toy. The shelf’s falling over will thwart the tiger’s hard work. Critically, one of the dogs will have been on stage to witness and gain knowledge of the tiger’s attempts to reach the moose toy, and will therefore be negligently accidental in its behavior (i.e., it could have foreseen the negative consequences that its actions would have for the tiger). The other dog will not be on stage during the tiger’s attempts to reach the moose, and will therefore be truly accidental in its behavior (i.e., it could not have foreseen consequences).
After watching the truly and negligently accidental actors in the condition they are in, infants will have a choice between the two actors.

Hypotheses (required)
For each of the research questions listed in the previous section, provide one or multiple specific and testable hypotheses. Please state if the hypotheses are directional or non-directional. If directional, state the direction. A predicted effect is also appropriate here.
These hypotheses are non-directional. If there is an asymmetry in infants’ evaluations of negligently accidental help and harm as in Woo et al. (under revised review), infants may prefer a truly accidental over a negligently accidental harmer, but not distinguish between truly and negligently accidental helpers. However, if our past finding that infants did not distinguish between truly and negligently accidental helpers was a statistical fluke, infants may prefer a negligently accidental over a truly accidental helper.
Sampling Plan
Existing Data (required)
Preregistration is designed to make clear the distinction between confirmatory tests, specified prior to seeing the data, and exploratory analyses conducted after observing the data. Therefore, creating a research plan in which existing data will be used presents unique challenges. Please select the description that best describes your situation. Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have questions about how to answer this question (prereg@cos.io).

●	Registration prior to creation of data
○

Explanation of existing data (required)
If you indicate that you will be using some data that already exist in this study, please describe the steps you have taken to assure that you are unaware of any patterns or summary statistics in the data. This may include an explanation of how access to the data has been limited, who has observed the data, or how you have avoided observing any analysis of the specific data you will use in your study. The purpose of this question is to assure that the line between confirmatory and exploratory analysis is clear.

We have run a single baby already, but we cannot really make assessments of patterns or summary statistics based on this one baby. 
Data collection procedures (required)
Please describe the process by which you will collect your data. If you are using human subjects, this should include the population from which you obtain subjects, recruitment efforts, payment for participation, how subjects will be selected for eligibility from the initial pool (e.g. inclusion and exclusion rules), and your study timeline. For studies that don’t include human subjects, include information about how you will collect samples, duration of data gathering efforts, source or location of samples, or batch numbers you will use.
Our population is composed of healthy full-term infants from the age of 9.5 to 10.5 months old from the Greater Vancouver area in Canada. Participants are initially recruited into a participant database from the hospital, community sign-ups, web sign-up, or word-of-mouth; research assistants contact participants' parents when they are eligible for this study. Participants and their parents do not receive monetary compensation, although they receive a certificate of participation, a toy or prize (e.g., a rubber ducky or a t-shirt), bus fare (if needed), and a free parking spot (if necessary). Data exclusions are standard in our lab and are detailed in the relevant section below. We aim to complete this study in about a year.
Sample size (required)
Describe the sample size of your study. How many units will be analyzed in the study? This could be the number of people, birds, classrooms, plots, interactions, or countries included. If the units are not individuals, then describe the size requirements for each unit. If you are using a clustered or multilevel design, how many units are you collecting at each level of the analysis?
We will have 64 infants, meaning there will be 32 infants in each of the help and harm conditions.
Sample size rationale (required)
This could include a power analysis or an arbitrary constraint such as time, money, or personnel.
Based on a power analysis of 80% for the harm condition in Woo et al. (under revised review), we determined the number of infants needed for each condition to replicate based on the harm condition. The sample size would have to be 31 infants for each condition, meaning 62 infants in total. We made the call to have 32 infants for each condition for counterbalancing purposes.
Stopping rule (required)
If your data collection procedures do not give you full control over your exact sample size, specify how you will decide when to terminate your data collection.
For each condition, we will stop the data collection at usable 32 babies. We anticipate an additional 30% of subjects will be run but not usable (see criteria below). 
Variables
Manipulated variables (required)
Describe all variables you plan to manipulate and the levels or treatment arms of each variable. For observational studies and meta-analyses, simply state that this is not applicable.
For each condition, we counterbalanced: sides of actor in show and choice, order of negligent versus truly accidental action, and color of negligent versus truly accidental actor (teal/purple).
Measured variables (required)
Describe each variable that you will measure. This will include outcome measures, as well as any predictors or covariates that you will measure. You do not need to include any variables that you plan on collecting if they are not going to be included in the confirmatory analyses of this study.
We will measure looking time after all events. Looking time was used to measure how infants were processing events. It may be that more unexpected events require longer times to process. Previous work has suggested no overall looking time differences between helpful and unhelpful events, or between truly accidental and negligently accidental events (see Woo et al., under revision); we expect the same results here. 
We will record a child's choice of an actor. Choice is presented by an experimenter blind to identity. The experimenter approaches the child on the parent’s lap (parent closes eyes) with the actors concealed behind his/her back, and says “hi” to get the child’s attention. Once the child looks at the experimenter, s/he presents the actors to the infant, holding one actor in each hand, initially out of the infant’s reach. The infant is required to look at both actors and back to the experimenter; after doing so, the experimenter moves the puppets within reach, and says, “Who do you like?”
Choice is determined by the first actor contacted via a visually guided reach and must occur within 2 minutes of character presentation. If the child is not attending to the characters: we reassure the child it is ok to choose, and we ask the parent to tell the child it is ok to choose without opening his/her eyes. 
Choices will be compared to chance via binomial and chi-square tests. We will check to ensure that there are no side preferences, order effects, or color preferences.
We will also examine data by age and gender.

Indices (required)
If any measurements are going to be combined into an index (or even a mean), what measures will you use and how will they be combined? Include either a formula or a precise description of your method. If your are using a more complicated statistical method to combine measures (e.g. a factor analysis), you can note that here but describe the exact method in the analysis plan section.
As is typical for infant studies, we will calculate mean values for looking times to identical events throughout the study. 
Design Plan
Study type (required)
Please check one of the following statements
●	Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
●	Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
●	Meta-Analysis - A systematic review of published studies.
●	Other

Blinding
Blinding describes who is aware of the experimental manipulations within a study. Mark all that apply.
●	No blinding is involved in this study.
●	For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
●	Research personnel who interact directly with the study subjects (either human or non-human subjects) will not be aware of the assigned treatments.
●	Research personnel who analyze the data collected from the study are not aware of the treatment applied to any given group.
●	Parents close their eyes for shows and for choice. 

Study design (required)
Describe your study design. Examples include two-group, factorial, randomized block, and repeated measures. Is it a between (unpaired), within-subject (paired), or mixed design? Describe any counterbalancing required. Typical study designs for observation studies include cohort, cross sectional, and case-control studies.
All babies of a single condition will see the same events. We may compare each baby's looking times and choice between the different characters.
Randomization (required)
If you are doing a randomized study, how will you randomize, and at what level?
We have counterbalanced several variables, which include: actor identity, actor side in show, actor presentation order, actor choice side. There will be 32 scripts per condition. A random number generator will assign babies to each script. Research assistants not involved in the running of participants choose scripts for the subsequent day’s studies; if the random number they generate corresponds to a used script, RAs choose the next largest script number of the same gender and if all scripts have been used start at the top of the counterbalancing sheet again. 
Analysis Plan
You may describe one or more confirmatory analysis in this preregistration. Please remember that all analyses specified below must be reported in the final article, and any additional analyses must be noted as exploratory or hypothesis-generating.

A confirmatory analysis plan must state up front which variables are predictors (independent) and which are the outcomes (dependent), otherwise it is an exploratory analysis. You are allowed to describe any exploratory work here, but a clear confirmatory analysis is required.

Statistical models (required)
What statistical model will you use to test each hypothesis? Please include the type of model (e.g. ANOVA, multiple regression, SEM, etc) and the specification of the model (this includes each variable that will be included as predictors, outcomes, or covariates). Please specify any interactions that will be tested and remember that any test not included here must be noted as an exploratory test in your final article.
We will use a binomial probability test to determine if a significant number of babies is choosing one character over another in a single condition. 
We will use chi-square tests to compare conditions. We will also use chi-square tests to determine if there are side preferences, gender differences, or order effects.
We will use univariate ANOVAs to determine if there are significant differences in looking time after negligently accidental versus truly accidental helping and harming events (none are predicted). We will also explore whether babies’ attention to negligently accidental and truly accidental helping and harming events influences their choices (no influence predicted). 
Transformations (required)
If you plan on transforming, centering, recoding the data, or will require a coding scheme for categorical variables, please describe that process.
As recently suggested by Csibra et al. (2016), we will log transform our looking time data before analyses so to correct for positive skew. 
Follow-up analyses (required)
If not specified previously, will you be conducting any confirmatory analyses to follow up on effects in your statistical model, such as subgroup analyses, pairwise or complex contrasts, or follow-up tests from interactions? Remember that any analyses not specified in this research plan must be noted as exploratory.
	None. 
Inference criteria (required)
What criteria will you use to make inferences? Please describe the information you’ll use (e.g. specify the p-values, Bayes factors, specific model fit indices), as well as cut-off criterion, where appropriate. Will you be using one or two tailed tests for each of your analyses? If you are comparing multiple conditions or testing multiple hypotheses, will you account for this?
We will use p-values, with a cut-off criterion of .05. We will use two-tailed tests. 
Data exclusion (required)
How will you determine which data points or samples (if any) to exclude from your analyses? How will outliers be handled?
We exclude data if participants are fussy, if participants are inattentive, if parents interfere, if there is a procedural error, if infants fail to choose a character, or if equipment fails.
Fussiness criteria includes: 
(i) distress that includes continued crying and tears. This always counts as a fuss-out, independently of parental decision. A blind experimenter (the coder) decides if the child meets this criterion.
(ii) mild distress that is followed by us asking the parent whether they would like to continue or not. Parental decision is used here. 
Trials are repeated if infants did not attend during the “critical” period (i.e., the part that makes a helper trial different from a hinderer trial). Infants are ruled “inattentive” and excluded from the final sample if they refuse to attend to our displays for over 2 minutes. 
Parental interference includes parents wishing to stop the study for reasons other than fussiness, parents doing something that might bias their child’s responses (e.g., emotional reactions after events; speaking to their babies about the events, telling their baby to choose the nice one, opening their eyes during choice, etc.). If parents do mild interfering things that would not necessarily bias their children (e.g., telling them to watch the show in a general sense; distracting the child during the show, etc.) experimenters will ask parents to stop and if they do stop the data will be included in the final sample. 
Procedural errors may include a supposedly blind experimenter becoming unblinded, deviation from standard procedure, and the choice procedure being performed incorrectly (e.g., stopping before a visually guided reach has occurred; not getting infants to attend to the center before characters are presented; if presentation is uneven in some way like the puppets are off-center etc.). All of these are determined by experimenters who do not know what the choice result was. 
Infants are considered to have failed to make a choice if the time to make a choice is equal to or greater than 2 minutes, or if they do not choose a character.
Equipment failure may occur if the computer for coding malfunctions such that a participant cannot be tested completely.
Missing data (required)

We should not have incomplete data. We run experiments to completion. If data of one child is missing (e.g., we wanted to confirm data points and realized the video was gone), we will replace the child’s data with data from a new participant.

If you plan to explore your data set to look for unexpected differences or relationships, you may describe those tests here. An exploratory test is any test where a prediction is not made up front, or there are multiple possible tests that you are going to use. A statistically significant finding in an exploratory test is a great way to form a new confirmatory hypothesis, which could be registered at a later time.
None.
Scripts
The purpose of a fully commented analysis script is to unambiguously provide the responses to all of the questions raised in the analysis section. This step is not common, but we encourage you to try creating an analysis script, refine it using a modeled dataset, and use it in place of your written analysis plan.

This optional step is helpful in order to create a process that is completely transparent and increase the likelihood that your analysis can be replicated. We recommend that you run the code on a simulated dataset in order to check that it will run without errors.
This is not necessary for our very simple data analyses.

title_r: The impact of perceived partisanship on climate policy support: A conceptual replication and extension of the temporal framing effect
abstract_r: Bridging the political divide between liberals and conservatives is one of the biggest challenges for broad public support of climate policies. Previous research has suggested that framing climate policies with respect to the past may reduce opposition by political conservatives, but recent attempts to replicate this effect have failed. Taking the influence of temporal framing on individuals' perception of the messenger into account may offer a new perspective on these inconsistent findings. To pursue this idea, the present work investigated how implicit cues contained in climate message framing as well as explicit political identity cues shape the perceived political orientation of a messenger and subsequent climate policy support by partisans. Across three experiments ($N_{total} = 2012$), we found that past (vs. future) framing and conservative (vs. liberal) party affiliation independently contributed to the messenger being perceived as more conservative. Past framing and conservative party affiliation increased endorsement of the messenger and the message by conservatives, but decreased endorsement by liberals. While past framing and conservative party affiliation independently increased conservatives' climate policy support (with no negative effects on liberals), only the combination of both cues entirely attenuated the negative relationship between conservatism and climate policy support. Moreover, temporal framing effects only emerged when messenger party affiliation was made explicit, suggesting that explicit cues may facilitate the integration of implicit identity cues contained in temporal framings. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of our integrated account, which reconciles some of the ambiguity in previous findings of temporal framing effects.

title_r: Merging Structural and Process-Related Approaches to the Study of Agreeableness: A Preregistered Replication and Extension
abstract_r: Agreeableness is one of the major domains included within prominent hierarchical models of personality like the Five-factor Model (FFM). (Low) agreeableness has shown to be the strongest correlate of a variety of antisocial behaviors relative to the other FFM domains. Though there is substantial evidence that (low) agreeableness is arguably the most important personality correlate of various antisocial behaviors, this evidence is descriptive and provides little information on the direction or processes underlying the relation. Process-related research has started to provide more insight into how agreeableness-related traits give rise to various antisocial and prosocial behaviors. The proposed study looks to first replicate previous research on some of the potential cognitive/emotional processes related to agreeableness, and then to conduct exploratory analyses to identify which, if any, of the empirically identified facets of agreeableness bear specific relations to the processes under study. Thus, the proposed project seeks to merge developments across important domains of personality research, structural research and process-based research, while also making use of open-science practices.

title_r: More or Less Violence in Schools? A Replication Study from 1996-2014 in Saxon Schools
abstract_r: Der verbreiteten Annahme einer ständigen Gewaltzunahme an Schulen stehen bisher nur wenige Studien im Zeitvergleich gegenüber. Der vorliegende Beitrag will diese Lücke schließen, indem er Ergebnisse einer aktuellen Replikationsstudie vorstellt und damit die Frage beantwortet, ob die Gewalt an Schulen im Vergleich zur Mitte der 1990er Jahre zu- oder abgenommen hat. Anhand einer repräsentativen sächsischen Stichprobe zeigt sich, dass im Jahr 2014 im Vergleich zu 1996 über weniger Gewalt an Schulen berichtet wird. Dies betrifft die Gewalt unter Schü ler(inne)n und die Gewalt gegen Lehrkräfte. Parallel hat die Interventionsbereitschaft unter der Lehrer- und Schülerschaft zugenommen. Zugleich macht die Studie auf differente Entwicklungstrends zwischen den Schülergruppen aufmerksam. Trotz eines insgesamt niedrigen Gewaltniveaus im Vergleich zur Mitte der 1990er Jahre legen die Befunde den Schluss nahe, bei den Präventionsbemühungen nicht nachzulassen. Veryfew studies have investigated the widely held assumption that violence in schools has constantly increased in recent years. The current study aims to fill this gap by presenting results of a recent replication study in Germany, as well as answering the question as to whether violence in schools increased or decreased in comparison with the mid-1990s. Based on a representative sample of Saxon students, this study shows that less violence was reported in schools in 2014 compared to 1996. This relates to both violence among students and their violent actions against teachers. Moreover, the willingness of teachers and students to intervene has increased. At the same time, this study draws attention to developmental trends between groups of students. Despite a general low level of violence in schools compared to the mid-1990s, the findings suggest that prevention efforts must be continued.
